keys.guide.arch.b1: Control plane: User → UI → HTTP API → Lab Service → ProjectStore/DAG; Host is the single source of truth.
keys.guide.arch.b2: Execution plane: Runtime drives DSH worker subagents; workers use tools/LLM; GitEngine owns branches/worktrees/commits.
keys.guide.arch.b3: Resource plane: Scheduler keeps the ready queue; Coordinator keeps lease queue/quota; GPU Fleet + NFS host remote containers.
keys.guide.arch.b4: Data plane: DAG/reports/events persist in ProjectStore; branches/commits live in Git; LLM/tool calls happen only agent-side.
keys.guide.arch.benefit: See how the whole system fits together
keys.guide.arch.lead: For technical readers: this is the full data/control flow. The Lab panel is only the entry point; Host is the authority for state and scheduling; agents execute in DSH sessions; Coordinator/Fleet turn whole-GPU leases into remote compute. Use “Next” below to light up each flow.
keys.guide.arch.step1.desc: You write the research goal and root prompt in the Lab panel. The request goes through HTTP API to Lab Service; ProjectStore writes the project, root node, and an empty DAG; GitEngine creates the root branch/worktree from the base commit. The node is planned.
keys.guide.arch.step1.title: ① Create project: prompt → root node
keys.guide.arch.step2.desc: Runtime/Orchestrator hands the root node to a worker subagent: isolated DSH session, cwd in the root worktree, prompt/constraints/time box injected. Host records the run and the agent starts.
keys.guide.arch.step2.title: ② Start root: Runtime creates an Agent
keys.guide.arch.step3.desc: The worker finishes the experiment in its worktree, commits code, and sends a structured report/metrics back to Host. ProjectStore updates node status, attempts, and report; the DAG root becomes completed and enters the review candidate set.
keys.guide.arch.step3.title: ③ Node completes: report + commit
keys.guide.arch.step4.desc: Advisor/Reviewer subagents read the report and project snapshot through a read-only context and return successor proposals. Host validates and writes child nodes + parent edges into the DAG; new nodes become planned and enter the ready queue. Agents never write the DAG directly.
keys.guide.arch.step4.title: ④ Expert review: report → child nodes
keys.guide.arch.step5.desc: The scheduler scans DAG-ready planned nodes and deterministically selects by resource pool, maxRunningNodes, and priority. Selected nodes become reserved and go to Runtime; nodes without resources stay in the waiting queue. The scheduler orders work; it does not execute experiments.
keys.guide.arch.step5.title: ⑤ Scheduler: pick from the ready queue
keys.guide.arch.step6.desc: The scheduler asks the Coordinator for resources. The Coordinator maintains a lease queue, project quotas, and cluster priority; on success it assigns a GPU Fleet machine/container and mounts the shared NFS worktree; otherwise the request keeps waiting.
keys.guide.arch.step6.title: ⑥ Coordinator: request a whole-GPU lease
keys.guide.arch.step7.desc: The worker runs the child experiment from its parent commit in the child worktree, creates a new commit, and returns a report. GitEngine records branch/commit history; the DAG node moves running → completed and the DAG grows a new experiment branch.
keys.guide.arch.step7.title: ⑦ Execute child: Git version iteration
keys.guide.arch.step8.desc: Auto mode repeats complete → review → propose → schedule → execute, growing the DAG deeper and wider; confirm mode pauses at approve/reject. A merge node joins successful branches, and you decide the final merge/push back to the Git Repo.
keys.guide.arch.step8.title: ⑧ Auto loop: DAG growth and human choices
keys.guide.arch.title: Full architecture: from a prompt to DAG growth
keys.guide.demo.b1: Manual mode: you start nodes and approve successor proposals from the expert group.
keys.guide.demo.b2: Auto mode: after expert review, Host creates and schedules successors automatically.
keys.guide.demo.b3: Native interaction record: every node has its own DSH session and Trajectory.
keys.guide.demo.b4: All nodes, logs, and traces are demo data, safe to replay repeatedly.
keys.guide.demo.benefit: See the full interaction without calling an LLM
keys.guide.demo.eventsHint: Click a canvas node for details
keys.guide.demo.lead: This page shrinks the Lab workbench into an interactive simulation: create a root node, start it manually, inspect the interaction record, switch to auto mode, and watch the DAG grow. No LLM calls; no real project changes.
keys.guide.demo.step1.desc: Create a project, write the research goal and root prompt; the Lab panel creates a root node and the DAG has exactly one planned node.
keys.guide.demo.step1.title: ① Create the initial node
keys.guide.demo.step2.desc: You click Start; Host creates a worker session, root becomes running, and executes in its own worktree.
keys.guide.demo.step2.title: ② Start the root manually
keys.guide.demo.step3.desc: The worker commits code + a report and root becomes completed; there are no successors yet, so the DAG stays a single node.
keys.guide.demo.step3.title: ③ Complete with a report
keys.guide.demo.step4.desc: Advisor/reviewer read the report and propose two experiments; Host writes child nodes + parent edges, so the DAG starts branching.
keys.guide.demo.step4.title: ④ Expert group proposes children
keys.guide.demo.step5.desc: In manual mode you approve one successor; it becomes running while the other stays planned, waiting for your decision.
keys.guide.demo.step5.title: ⑤ Approve and execute manually
keys.guide.demo.step6.desc: Open the native Trajectory mock to see the prompt, tool calls, commit, and report; in the real system this is the DSH session.
keys.guide.demo.step6.title: ⑥ Inspect the interaction record
keys.guide.demo.step7.desc: Enable auto: review → create successors → schedule automatically; more nodes appear and the DAG keeps growing.
keys.guide.demo.step7.title: ⑦ Switch to auto mode
keys.guide.demo.step8.desc: Multiple branches run in parallel with completed/running states in one graph; merge nodes and human trade-offs remain under your control.
keys.guide.demo.step8.title: ⑧ DAG growth result
keys.guide.demo.title: Walk through the real UI inside the guide

keys.guide.label.question: Research question
keys.guide.page1.b1: Every node carries its goal, constraints, resources, and time box; an agent executes it in an isolated environment.
keys.guide.page1.b2: Code, reports, and failure evidence are archived automatically; the next experiment continues from existing results.
keys.guide.page1.b3: From “let me try this” to “evidence-backed next step”, without the gap in between.
keys.guide.page1.lead: Write down your research question; the platform turns it into a bounded, trackable, reviewable experiment node — no more manual environments, command logs, or lost results.
keys.guide.page1.title: Do not let a good idea stop at a script
keys.guide.page2.b1: No manual commits: each experiment result enters the commit history automatically.
keys.guide.page2.b2: Parallel experiments do not trample each other; compare, revert, and reproduce anytime.
keys.guide.page2.b3: Successful experiments can converge through a merge node into one reliable conclusion.
keys.guide.page2.benefit: Experiments do not pollute each other
keys.guide.page2.lead: The project binds one Git repo; each node gets an isolated worktree and branch. The parent result is the child starting point.
keys.guide.page2.title: Every experiment gets its own clean workbench
keys.guide.page3.b1: One parent can grow multiple parallel experiment branches.
keys.guide.page3.b2: Successes and failures stay in the lineage; failure is evidence for the next experiment.
keys.guide.page3.b3: You do not need to draw the whole tree up front; the system keeps growing it with results.
keys.guide.page3.lead: One result can inspire several new hypotheses; the DAG records “who continues from whose result”, making the whole research path visible.
keys.guide.page3.title: Experiments are not a line; they are a branching tree
keys.guide.page4.b1: Every node has a hard time box; timeouts terminate deterministically instead of hanging forever.
keys.guide.page4.b2: Nodes run up to the concurrency limit; the rest queue automatically.
keys.guide.page4.b3: Open the native trajectory anytime to see live reasoning, tool calls, and reports.
keys.guide.page4.lead: Nodes execute asynchronously in the background; no terminal watching. The Host owns timeouts, state, reports, and commits, and you return only when a judgement is needed.
keys.guide.page4.title: After starting it, you can go grab a coffee
keys.guide.page5.b1: A project resource pool is an explicit ledger, for example gpu=2.
keys.guide.page5.b2: The scheduler decides order; workers execute. Clear responsibility boundaries.
keys.guide.page5.b3: Queues and quotas keep multiple experiments from exhausting the same resource at once.
keys.guide.page5.lead: Nodes are planned first; the scheduler then orders execution by resource pools and priority. Insufficient resources mean waiting, not failing.
keys.guide.page5.title: Resources are limited; experiments do not have to fight
keys.guide.page6.b1: Project quotas plus cluster priority share GPUs fairly across projects.
keys.guide.page6.b2: Fleet executes over SSH + containers on remote hosts, with worktrees on shared NFS.
keys.guide.page6.b3: Exclusive whole-GPU leases make results attributable and reproducible.
keys.guide.page6.benefit: From one machine to the whole cluster
keys.guide.page6.lead: The coordinator grants whole-GPU leases; a node requests before it starts and queues if it must. The control host can have no GPU; compute happens on remote machines.
keys.guide.page6.title: No local GPU? Turn the cluster into your workbench
keys.guide.page7.b1: Auto mode loops review → propose → execute; confirm mode asks you to approve or reject first.
keys.guide.page7.b2: Failures are stopped and cleaned up; retry, use a stronger model, or abandon the branch.
keys.guide.page7.b3: A merge node combines multiple successful paths into one conclusion.
keys.guide.page7.lead: Advisors and reviewers read completed reports and propose successors; the scheduler starts only resource-eligible nodes. You keep the direction and risk trade-offs.
keys.guide.page7.title: AI proposes the next step; you set the direction
keys.guide.page8.b1: ① Create a project: bind a repo, write the research goal and root node.
keys.guide.page8.b2: ② Start/auto: let nodes run asynchronously; read reports and trajectories.
keys.guide.page8.b3: ③ Review/merge: approve successors, merge results, push code.
keys.guide.page8.b4: Open the project Copilot anytime to discuss the whole project and next steps.
keys.guide.page8.lead: Treat the platform as a workbench that grows an experiment lineage by itself, not as a chat bot.
keys.guide.page8.title: Give direction, collect results, make choices
